problem: Employee asks when salary must be paid after month-end
symptoms: Question from HR/payroll about legal salary due date and regular payday timing in Czech Republic
analysis: Likely HR/payroll compliance query. Czech Labour Code §141 defines salary is payable after work is performed, no later than in the following calendar month, and regular payday must be set.
solution: Inform requester that salary/wage must be paid after work is performed, no later than in the calendar month following the month when entitlement arose. Regular payday must be defined by employer. If payday falls during vacation, salary should be paid before vacation or via agreed alternate date.

problem: Employee on vacation asks if salary can be paid later because payroll run is delayed
symptoms: Payroll deadline collides with employee vacation period
analysis: Czech Labour Code §141 addresses payday during vacation. Employer should pay before vacation if payday falls into vacation period, or provide advance if exact calculation is not possible.
solution: If regular payday falls during employee vacation, pay salary before vacation unless another date is agreed. If payroll cannot be fully calculated in time, pay a reasonable advance and settle the remaining part on the next regular payday after vacation.

problem: Manager asks whether lunch break counts as working time
symptoms: Dispute about 30-minute meal break recording in attendance system
analysis: Czech Labour Code §88: standard meal/rest break is generally not counted as working time. Special exception exists for non-interruptible work where adequate rest/meal time is provided and counted.
solution: Standard meal/rest breaks are not counted as working time. At least 30 minutes must be provided no later than after 6 hours of continuous work (4.5 hours for minors). If work cannot be interrupted, provide adequate rest/meal time without stopping operations and count that time as working time.

problem: Supervisor split employee break into two short breaks and asks if it is valid
symptoms: Break was divided into multiple parts; uncertainty about legal minimum
analysis: Czech Labour Code §88 allows split breaks, but at least one part must be at least 15 minutes.
solution: Break may be split, but at least one break segment must be 15 minutes or longer. Also ensure total meal/rest break rules are met and it is not placed at the very start or end of the shift.

problem: Employee says no break was provided during long shift
symptoms: Worked over 6 hours continuously without meal/rest break
analysis: Potential non-compliance with Czech Labour Code §88. Employer must provide meal/rest break no later than after 6 hours continuous work (4.5 hours for minors).
solution: Review shift schedule and attendance records. Ensure the employee receives a meal/rest break no later than after 6 hours of continuous work (4.5 hours for minors). Update scheduling and supervisor instructions to prevent recurrence.

problem: HR asks if safety break is counted into working time
symptoms: Job has mandatory safety breaks under special regulations
analysis: Czech Labour Code §89: safety breaks are counted as working time. If safety break overlaps meal/rest break, meal/rest break is also counted.
solution: Yes, safety breaks required by special regulations are counted as working time. If a safety break overlaps with a meal/rest break, the meal/rest break is also counted as working time for that overlapping period.

problem: Employee asks about minimum daily rest between shifts
symptoms: Shift planning issue with short interval between end and next start
analysis: Czech Labour Code §90 sets daily continuous rest (typically 11 hours in 24h, more for minors), with limited exceptions.
solution: Default rule: provide continuous daily rest of at least 11 hours within each 24-hour period (higher protections apply to minors). Only use shortened rest in specific legally allowed cases and compensate by extending the following rest period accordingly.

problem: HR asks how long salary compensation is paid during temporary sickness
symptoms: Question about first days of sick leave compensation and payroll processing
analysis: Czech Labour Code §192 and §193 govern compensation during first 14 calendar days (subject to conditions) and payroll document deadlines.
solution: For eligible employees, wage/salary compensation is paid during the first 14 calendar days of temporary incapacity or quarantine, for relevant working days/holidays under legal conditions. Process payment based on required sickness documents and communicate document submission deadline before payroll cutoff.

problem: Payroll cannot include sickness compensation because documents arrived late
symptoms: Employee provided temporary incapacity documents after payroll cutoff
analysis: Czech Labour Code §193 says employer sets deadline for document submission so compensation can be paid in that payroll term.
solution: Apply the internal payroll cutoff deadline for sickness documents. If documents arrived after cutoff, process compensation in the next regular payroll term and document the reason. Clearly communicate the cutoff date for future cases.

problem: Employee on DPP/DPČ asks whether sickness compensation applies
symptoms: Question about temporary incapacity while working under agreement outside employment contract
analysis: Czech Labour Code §194 extends compensation rules to DPP/DPČ under conditions tied to §192 and §193.
solution: Employees working under DPP/DPČ may be entitled to compensation during the first 14 calendar days of temporary incapacity/quarantine under conditions defined by the Labour Code and sickness insurance rules. Verify the specific agreement type and eligibility conditions before payroll processing.

problem: Employee requests parental leave and HR is unsure about notice timing
symptoms: Written request submitted shortly before requested parental leave start
analysis: Czech Labour Code §196: parental leave is granted on written request; request should generally be submitted at least 30 days in advance unless serious reasons prevent it.
solution: Require a written parental leave request stating the requested duration. Standard expectation is submission at least 30 days before start date, unless serious reasons on employee side prevented earlier submission. Grant leave up to the legal maximum period (generally until child reaches 3 years).

problem: Employee asks if father can start parental leave immediately after birth
symptoms: Father requests parental leave from date of child birth
analysis: Czech Labour Code §196 allows parental leave for father from birth, based on written request.
solution: Yes. The father may request parental leave from the child’s birth date, based on a written request specifying the requested leave period (within legal limits).

problem: Employee asks about maternity leave duration for twins
symptoms: HR needs to confirm maternity leave length for multiple birth
analysis: Czech Labour Code §195 sets maternity leave length to 28 weeks, or 37 weeks for birth of two or more children.
solution: Maternity leave is generally 28 weeks. If the employee gave birth to two or more children, maternity leave is 37 weeks, under the conditions set by the Labour Code.

problem: Employee asks about paternity leave entitlement
symptoms: Question whether employer must grant paternity leave
analysis: Czech Labour Code §195a requires employer to provide paternity leave in connection with birth and child care, tied to sickness insurance provisions.
solution: Employer must provide paternity leave in connection with the birth and care of a child, in the duration tied to the paternity benefit period under sickness insurance rules. Confirm required documents and requested dates.

problem: Payroll asks whether salary assignment to third party is allowed
symptoms: Employee wants salary claim transferred/assigned to someone else
analysis: Czech Labour Code §144a prohibits assignment of wage/salary claims and use as debt security, except specific statutory mechanisms (e.g., wage deductions agreement context).
solution: Do not allow assignment of the employee’s wage/salary claim to a third party. Wage/salary claims and compensation claims cannot be assigned or used as debt security, except where specific law allows (e.g., lawful deduction arrangements).

problem: Finance asks if employer can deduct a contractual penalty directly from salary
symptoms: Request to withhold amount from employee wage due to internal penalty
analysis: Czech Labour Code §146–147 prohibit arbitrary deductions; §147(3) explicitly disallows certain employer-favor deductions like contractual penalties.
solution: No. Do not deduct contractual penalties directly from salary. Wage deductions are allowed only in legally defined cases or based on a lawful wage deduction agreement, and contractual penalty deductions in favor of employer are not permitted.

problem: Payroll asks what may be deducted automatically from salary
symptoms: Need a checklist of lawful payroll deductions without separate employee consent
analysis: Czech Labour Code §147 lists statutory deductions such as tax, social/health insurance, certain returned advances, etc.
solution: Automatic deductions are limited to statutory items (e.g., income tax, social and health insurance contributions, and certain legally defined returned advances/overpayments). For anything else, verify a legal basis or a valid wage deduction agreement before processing.

problem: HR asks about order of wage deductions after employee joins from another employer
symptoms: New employer receives notice of existing wage deduction arrangement/execution
analysis: Czech Labour Code §149 preserves ordering in some cases and requires new employer to continue deductions once informed.
solution: If a valid wage deduction arrangement already existed, the order may remain preserved with the new employer. Once notified (by employee, prior employer, or entitled party), verify documentation and continue deductions according to legal priority rules.

problem: Payroll asks what records must be kept for wage deductions
symptoms: Audit/compliance preparation for deduction documentation
analysis: Czech Labour Code §150 requires employer to keep identifying data and documents related to wage deductions for the same retention period as wage records.
solution: Keep identification details of the entitled party (person/company) and all documents related to wage deductions, and retain them for the same period as other wage/payroll records.

problem: HR asks how to answer a general employee question about legal HR rights without giving legal advice
symptoms: Employees submit broad questions on leave, breaks, pay timing, deductions
analysis: Operational need: provide internal guidance and route legal-edge cases. Best practice is summarize policy and cite relevant Labour Code sections, escalate edge cases.
solution: Answer with internal policy guidance plus legal basis reference (e.g., relevant Labour Code section). If the case is non-standard (multiple contracts, disputes, court order, unclear documentation), escalate to HR lead or legal counsel and avoid definitive legal interpretation.
